setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which set of abilities must a patient demonstrate to have capacity for a specific treatment decision?

options.B: Have a normal GCS and no psychiatric history
options.C: Agree with the medical team's recommendation after hearing the risks and benefits
options.D: Be older than 65 years
options.E: Understand, retain, use or weigh the information, and communicate a decision

explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and requires the ability to understand, retain, weigh information and communicate a choice. Disagreement with medical advice does not imply incapacity. Capacity may fluctuate in critical illness, so reassessment is needed.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: How are withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment regarded in most ethical frameworks?

options.A: Withdrawing requires a court order in all cases
options.B: Withholding is permitted only in children
options.C: Withdrawing is always unethical once treatment has been started
options.D: Withholding is always unethical
options.E: As ethically equivalent; neither needs stronger justification

explanation: Most ethical and professional bodies consider withholding and withdrawing equivalent. Viewing withdrawal as more serious may discourage time-limited trials of treatment. Decisions should be based on the patient's values, goals and prognosis.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]; Downar et al. 2016 (withdrawal of life-sustaining measures) [55]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: During withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, a dying patient shows signs of distress. The physician gives titrated opioids and benzodiazepines, aware that they may shorten life. Which ethical principle supports this?

options.A: Euthanasia is permitted in all ICUs
options.D: The principle of distributive justice in allocating scarce ICU resources fairly
options.E: Double effect: the intention is to relieve suffering, not to hasten death

explanation: Doses of opioids and sedatives titrated to relieve symptoms are ethically appropriate even if they could hasten death, because the intended effect is comfort. Studies show appropriately titrated doses do not shorten survival. Doses should be proportionate and documented.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]; Downar et al. 2016 (withdrawal of life-sustaining measures) [55]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Why should neuromuscular blockers not be started or continued during withdrawal of mechanical ventilation?

options.D: They mask distress, preventing assessment of comfort, without any benefit
options.E: They prevent agonal breathing, which is always beneficial for the family

explanation: Neuromuscular blockers prevent the patient from showing distress and have no palliative benefit. Guidelines recommend allowing their effect to wear off (with monitoring) before withdrawal of ventilation, unless this would markedly prolong the dying process in exceptional circumstances.
referenceText: Downar et al. 2016 (withdrawal of life-sustaining measures) [55]; Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What did the trial by Lautrette and colleagues show about a structured end-of-life family conference (VALUE approach) with a bereavement brochure?

options.B: Fewer PTSD, anxiety and depression symptoms in relatives at 90 days
options.D: No effect on relatives' psychological outcomes at 90 days or at 1 year
options.E: Increased use of life-sustaining treatments

explanation: The VALUE mnemonic (Value what relatives say, Acknowledge emotions, Listen, Understand the patient as a person, Elicit questions) with longer family conferences and a brochure reduced PTSD, anxiety and depression symptoms among relatives.
referenceText: Lautrette et al. 2007 (family communication strategy) [125]; Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: When a patient lacks capacity and has no advance directive, what standard should surrogate decision-makers ideally apply?

options.C: Substituted judgement: what the patient would have chosen, given their values
options.D: The physician's personal values
options.E: Always the most aggressive treatment available, to preserve life at all costs

explanation: Surrogates should use substituted judgement, reflecting the patient's values and previously expressed wishes. When these are unknown, the best interests standard applies. Clinicians support surrogates by providing information and recommendations.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A family requests continued full ICU support for a patient with irreversible multiorgan failure, which the team considers non-beneficial. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Ongoing communication, second opinions, ethics input and a fair process, with transfer options
options.B: Unilateral immediate withdrawal of treatment without any further discussion with the family
options.C: Transfer to a ward without informing the family
options.D: Ask the family to leave the hospital
options.E: Always continue all treatment indefinitely

explanation: Professional statements recommend a stepwise process for disputes about potentially inappropriate treatment: early and repeated communication, palliative care involvement, second opinions, ethics committee review and, if needed, offering transfer. Legal frameworks differ between countries, including Egypt.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]; Downar et al. 2016 (withdrawal of life-sustaining measures) [55]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which practice improves consent rates for organ donation after brain death?

options.B: Separating news of death from the donation request, involving a trained specialist
options.C: Combining the news of death and the donation request in one sentence to save time
options.D: Having the treating surgeon request donation during resuscitation
options.E: Asking for donation before brain death testing begins

explanation: Decoupling the explanation of death from the request for donation and involving trained requesters (e.g. specialist nurses) increase consent. Discussions should be planned, culturally sensitive and respectful of religious beliefs, which are important in Egypt and the region.
referenceText: Kotloff et al. 2015 (management of the potential organ donor) [118]; Greer et al. 2020 (World Brain Death Project) [83]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In controlled donation after circulatory death, what is the role of the "no-touch" period after circulatory arrest?

options.A: A period during which heparin is withheld
options.B: A mandated observation period (commonly 5 minutes) confirming permanent cessation of circulation
options.C: A period after which organs may be retrieved without formally declaring death by any criteria
options.D: A period during which CPR is attempted
options.E: A period to allow family to request ECMO

explanation: Death is confirmed after an observation period without circulation (commonly 2–5 minutes, 5 minutes in the UK and many countries) to ensure that auto-resuscitation does not occur. Retrieval teams must not be involved in the decision to withdraw treatment or in declaring death.
referenceText: Kotloff et al. 2015 (management of the potential organ donor) [118]; Downar et al. 2016 (withdrawal of life-sustaining measures) [55]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A previously competent patient has a valid written advance directive refusing mechanical ventilation in the event of terminal illness. He now lacks capacity and has terminal respiratory failure. What should the team do?

options.A: Intubate because the family disagrees with the directive
options.B: Respect the advance directive, providing comfort-focused care
options.C: Provide ventilation for 7 days and then follow the directive
options.D: Seek a court order to intubate
options.E: Ignore the directive because he cannot confirm it now

explanation: A valid and applicable advance refusal of treatment has the same force as a contemporaneous decision by a competent patient in many jurisdictions. Clinicians must check that it applies to the current situation; comfort care continues.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which measure is recommended when planning terminal (palliative) extubation?

options.C: Anticipatory drugs for dyspnoea and secretions, and preparing the family
options.D: Performing extubation without informing the family
options.E: Withholding opioids to avoid hastening death, even if the patient is dyspnoeic

explanation: Palliative extubation requires preparation: discussing what to expect, stopping monitoring alarms, titrating opioids and sedatives to comfort, and giving antisecretory agents (e.g. glycopyrrolate) to reduce noisy breathing. Agonal breathing is managed with comfort measures.
referenceText: Downar et al. 2016 (withdrawal of life-sustaining measures) [55]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: During a surge when ICU beds are insufficient, which principle should guide triage decisions?

options.A: First-come, first-served regardless of prognosis, likelihood of benefit or comorbidity
options.B: Transparent, consistent benefit-based criteria applied by a separate triage team
options.C: Decisions by the most junior doctor available
options.D: Age as the sole criterion
options.E: Social status or ability to pay

explanation: Ethical triage in crises uses objective, transparent criteria based on likelihood of survival and benefit, applied equally, with regular review and appeals. Separating triage officers from bedside clinicians reduces moral distress and bias.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]; Valentin & Ferdinande 2011 (ESICM ICU requirements) [221]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What did the systematic review by Pronovost and colleagues show about high-intensity ICU physician staffing (intensivist-led care)?

options.A: Lower ICU and hospital mortality and shorter stay
options.D: Increased costs without any benefit in outcome
options.E: No effect on outcomes

explanation: High-intensity staffing (mandatory intensivist consultation or closed ICU) was associated with reduced ICU and hospital mortality and shorter stays. ESICM recommends intensivist-led units with adequate nursing ratios, typically 1:1 for ventilated patients.
referenceText: Pronovost et al. 2002 (ICU physician staffing) [172]; Valentin & Ferdinande 2011 (ESICM ICU requirements) [221]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What did the Keystone ICU project in Michigan demonstrate?

options.C: Antibiotic-impregnated catheters alone eliminated bloodstream infections in all units
options.D: Only expensive technology reduced infections
options.E: An evidence-based checklist and safety culture markedly reduced CRBSI rates

explanation: The Keystone project implemented five evidence-based practices for line insertion (hand hygiene, full barrier precautions, chlorhexidine, avoiding the femoral site, removing unnecessary catheters) with a checklist and culture change, reducing CRBSI rates by up to 66%, with sustained effects.
referenceText: Pronovost et al. 2006 (Keystone ICU project) [171]; Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which tool is commonly used to structure clinical communication and handover to reduce errors?

options.D: CURB-65
options.E: GCS

explanation: Structured communication tools such as SBAR improve the clarity of handovers and escalation, reducing omissions and adverse events. Communication failures are a leading contributor to serious incidents in healthcare.
referenceText: Valentin & Ferdinande 2011 (ESICM ICU requirements) [221]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: After a serious medication error causing harm, which approach is most appropriate to prevent recurrence?

options.A: Disciplining the nurse who administered the drug without investigation
options.B: Ignoring the error if the patient recovered
options.C: Root cause analysis focusing on systems rather than individual blame
options.D: Banning the drug from the hospital
options.E: Concealing the error from the patient

explanation: Root cause analysis identifies latent system failures (e.g. look-alike packaging, staffing, protocols). A just culture balances accountability with learning. Open disclosure to the patient and family is an ethical and professional obligation.
referenceText: Valentin & Ferdinande 2011 (ESICM ICU requirements) [221]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the main purpose of a rapid response (medical emergency) team?

options.B: Early review of deteriorating ward patients by set criteria, to prevent arrest and ICU admission
options.D: To decide on discharge from hospital
options.E: To replace the cardiac arrest team for all in-hospital resuscitation calls and patient transfers

explanation: Rapid response systems use track-and-trigger criteria (e.g. NEWS) to identify physiological deterioration and summon a critical care-skilled team. They are associated with reduced in-hospital cardiac arrests and may identify patients needing treatment limitation discussions.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Valentin & Ferdinande 2011 (ESICM ICU requirements) [221]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which components contribute to the APACHE II score?

options.A: Daily organ dysfunction scores over the whole ICU stay, plus age and admission diagnosis
options.B: Length of hospital stay before ICU
options.C: Worst acute physiology in the first 24 hours, plus age and chronic health points
options.D: SOFA score plus age
options.E: Only the admission diagnosis

explanation: APACHE II combines 12 physiological variables (worst values in the first 24 hours), age points and chronic health points (total score 0–71). Combined with diagnostic category, it predicts hospital mortality for groups, not individuals.
referenceText: Knaus et al. 1985 (APACHE II) [116]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: An ICU had 120 deaths in a year, while the severity-adjusted model predicted 150 deaths. What is the standardised mortality ratio?
explanation: SMR = observed deaths / expected deaths = 120 / 150 = 0.8, suggesting fewer deaths than predicted. Interpretation requires a well-calibrated model for the population; differences in case mix, lead-time bias and coding affect SMRs.
referenceText: Knaus et al. 1985 (APACHE II) [116]; Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A new test is evaluated in 300 patients: 100 have the disease, of whom 90 test positive; 200 do not, of whom 180 test negative. What is the positive predictive value?

options.D: About 90%
options.E: About 95%

explanation: True positives = 90, false positives = 200 − 180 = 20. PPV = 90 / (90 + 20) ≈ 82%. Sensitivity = 90/100 = 90% and specificity = 180/200 = 90%. PPV depends on disease prevalence, which here is 33%.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: How does a fall in disease prevalence affect the predictive values of a test with fixed sensitivity and specificity?

options.D: Both predictive values rise
options.E: Predictive values are unaffected by prevalence

explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test; predictive values depend on prevalence. In low-prevalence populations, more positive results are false positives, so PPV falls and NPV rises.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%. What is the positive likelihood ratio?
explanation: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) = 0.9 / 0.1 = 9. Likelihood ratios above 10 or below 0.1 generate large changes from pre-test to post-test probability. LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity = 0.1 / 0.9 ≈ 0.11.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In a trial, mortality is 30% in the control group and 25% in the treatment group. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one death?
explanation: Absolute risk reduction = 30% − 25% = 5% (0.05). NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.05 = 20. The relative risk reduction is 5/30 ≈ 17%, which can make an effect seem larger than the absolute benefit.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Using the same trial (control mortality 30%, treatment mortality 25%), what is the relative risk reduction?

options.D: About 30%
options.E: About 83%

explanation: Relative risk = 0.25 / 0.30 ≈ 0.83, so relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.83 ≈ 17% (or ARR/control risk = 0.05/0.30). Reporting relative and absolute effects together aids interpretation.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In a randomised trial, what is a type I error?

options.C: Failing to detect a real treatment effect (false negative), with probability beta
options.D: Concluding an effect exists when it does not (false positive), with probability alpha
options.E: Bias due to loss of follow-up

explanation: Type I error (alpha, commonly 0.05) is rejecting a true null hypothesis. Type II error (beta) is failing to reject a false null hypothesis; power = 1 − beta (commonly 80–90%). Multiple comparisons inflate type I error.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]; Hulley et al. 2013 (Designing Clinical Research) [97]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which change increases the statistical power of a trial, all else being equal?

options.D: Increasing outcome variability
options.E: Reducing the expected effect size

explanation: Power increases with larger sample size, larger true effect size, higher alpha and lower variability. Many critical care trials have been underpowered because of optimistic effect size assumptions, resulting in "negative" trials that cannot exclude clinically important effects.
referenceText: Hulley et al. 2013 (Designing Clinical Research) [97]; Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Why is intention-to-treat analysis preferred in randomised controlled trials?

options.A: It preserves randomisation by analysing patients in their assigned groups
options.B: It excludes patients who did not receive the allocated treatment as planned
options.C: It is only used in non-inferiority trials
options.D: It always shows larger treatment effects
options.E: It eliminates the need for blinding

explanation: Intention-to-treat analysis maintains comparability between groups and reflects real-world effectiveness, avoiding bias from non-adherence or crossover. Per-protocol analyses are often reported as supportive, particularly in non-inferiority trials.
referenceText: Hulley et al. 2013 (Designing Clinical Research) [97]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In a non-inferiority trial, how is non-inferiority concluded?

options.C: The trial includes more than 1000 patients
options.D: The p-value for superiority is below 0.05 in both the per-protocol and as-treated analyses
options.E: The CI upper bound for the difference in harm lies below the pre-specified margin

explanation: Non-inferiority is shown when the confidence interval for the treatment difference excludes the pre-specified margin of clinically acceptable inferiority. The margin should be justified clinically; per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses should both support the conclusion.
referenceText: Hulley et al. 2013 (Designing Clinical Research) [97]; Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A trial reports a relative risk of death of 0.85 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.70 to 1.03. How should this be interpreted?

options.C: The confidence interval is too narrow to interpret, so the trial result is inconclusive overall
options.D: The trial proves no effect exists
options.E: Not significant at 5%, since the interval includes 1.0, but important benefit is not excluded

explanation: A 95% CI including 1.0 for a ratio measure indicates no statistically significant difference. The interval is compatible with a 30% reduction to a 3% increase in risk; "absence of evidence is not evidence of absence".
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: When does the odds ratio approximate the relative risk?

options.C: Only in case–control studies with common outcomes
options.D: When the outcome is rare (e.g. below about 10%)
options.E: Always, regardless of incidence

explanation: For rare outcomes, odds and risks are similar, so the OR approximates the RR. For common outcomes (as in many ICU studies, e.g. mortality of 30%), the OR exaggerates the RR. Case–control studies can only estimate ORs.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which method compares time-to-event outcomes between groups while adjusting for covariates?

options.D: Kappa statistic
options.E: Cox proportional hazards regression

explanation: Cox regression estimates hazard ratios for time-to-event data while adjusting for covariates, assuming proportional hazards. Kaplan–Meier curves describe survival, and the log-rank test compares curves without adjustment.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In an observational study, patients given a drug were sicker than those who were not, and the drug appeared to increase mortality. What type of bias is most likely?

options.A: Observer bias in a blinded trial
options.D: Confounding by indication
options.E: Recall bias

explanation: Confounding by indication occurs when the reason for receiving a treatment (e.g. severity) is itself associated with the outcome. Randomisation, multivariable adjustment, propensity scores and instrumental variables address it, though residual confounding may persist in observational studies.
referenceText: Hulley et al. 2013 (Designing Clinical Research) [97]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In a meta-analysis, the I² statistic is 75%. What does this indicate?

options.C: The included studies all used identical methods, populations and outcome definitions
options.D: Substantial heterogeneity beyond chance, warranting caution and exploration
options.E: The pooled effect is definitely correct

explanation: I² estimates the proportion of variability between studies due to heterogeneity rather than chance; values above about 50–75% indicate substantial heterogeneity. Random-effects models, subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses should be considered.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What distinguishes a pragmatic trial from an explanatory trial?

options.B: Pragmatic trials test effectiveness in usual care with broad eligibility; explanatory trials test efficacy
options.D: Pragmatic trials are always unblinded and unrandomised, whereas explanatory trials are always blinded
options.E: Explanatory trials do not use control groups

explanation: Pragmatic trials (e.g. many ICU fluid trials) emphasise generalisability with broad inclusion and usual-care comparators. Explanatory trials maximise internal validity with strict protocols. Most trials lie on a continuum (PRECIS-2 tool).
referenceText: Hulley et al. 2013 (Designing Clinical Research) [97]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What does an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.5 indicate?

options.D: The test is twice as good as chance
options.E: The test discriminates no better than chance

explanation: The AUROC summarises discrimination across thresholds: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is chance. Values of 0.7–0.8 are acceptable and above 0.8 good. Calibration (agreement between predicted and observed risk) is assessed separately.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Why are some ICU trials cluster randomised (e.g. by unit rather than by patient)?

options.A: When the intervention acts at unit level or contamination between patients is likely
options.B: Because patient consent is never needed
options.C: To ensure blinding of all participants
options.D: To avoid ethical approval
options.E: To increase statistical power compared with randomising individual patients, at the same sample size

explanation: Cluster randomisation reduces contamination when interventions affect the whole unit (e.g. selective decontamination, staffing models). It requires larger samples because outcomes within clusters are correlated (intracluster correlation coefficient).
referenceText: Hulley et al. 2013 (Designing Clinical Research) [97]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What did the 3SITES trial show about central venous catheter insertion sites?

options.A: Subclavian had the lowest infection and DVT rates but more pneumothorax
options.B: Internal jugular placement had the highest pneumothorax risk of all sites
options.C: Femoral placement had the lowest infection risk
options.D: Subclavian placement had the highest infection risk
options.E: Site had no effect on complications

explanation: 3SITES randomised 3471 catheters; subclavian insertion had fewer bloodstream infections and symptomatic DVTs than jugular or femoral sites, but more pneumothoraces. Site selection balances these risks with operator expertise and patient factors.
referenceText: Parienti et al. 2015 (3SITES) [162]; Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the benefit of real-time ultrasound guidance for internal jugular vein cannulation?

options.A: Longer insertion time with more complications than the anatomical landmark technique
options.D: Higher first-attempt success and fewer arterial punctures than landmark technique
options.E: Increased pneumothorax risk

explanation: Cochrane analysis shows ultrasound guidance increases success, reduces the number of attempts and lowers arterial puncture and haematoma rates. Real-time guidance is recommended for jugular and femoral access.
referenceText: Brass et al. 2015 (ultrasound-guided internal jugular cannulation) [25]; Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: During internal jugular catheterisation, a 12-Fr dialysis dilator is inserted and the line is then found to be in the carotid artery. What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Remove the catheter immediately and apply firm pressure for 20 minutes
options.B: Leave it in place and get urgent vascular or endovascular input for removal
options.C: Ignore it and insert another line on the same side
options.D: Remove the catheter and anticoagulate
options.E: Use the catheter for infusions

explanation: Removing a large-bore catheter from an artery with pressure alone risks haemorrhage, airway compression, pseudoaneurysm and stroke. The catheter should be left in situ and removed under surgical or endovascular control. Confirming venous placement (ultrasound, manometry) before dilation prevents this complication.
referenceText: Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: During removal of an internal jugular catheter from a sitting patient, he suddenly becomes hypotensive, hypoxaemic and has a "mill-wheel" murmur. What is the immediate management?

options.D: Left lateral head-down position and 100% oxygen
options.E: Give thrombolysis

explanation: Venous air embolism occurs when air enters a central vein, often during insertion or removal with the patient upright or during inspiration. Left lateral Trendelenburg positioning traps air in the right atrium, oxygen reduces bubble size, and aspiration through a central line may help. Lines should be removed with the patient supine or head-down and an occlusive dressing applied.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A dyspnoeic patient has bilateral A-lines with lung sliding on lung ultrasound and a positive compression ultrasound for DVT. According to the BLUE protocol, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: ARDS
options.E: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema

explanation: The BLUE protocol uses lung ultrasound profiles: an A-profile (A-lines with sliding) plus DVT suggests PE; B-profile suggests pulmonary oedema; absent sliding with A-lines and lung point suggests pneumothorax; consolidation or asymmetric B-lines suggest pneumonia. A-profile without DVT suggests COPD or asthma.
referenceText: Lichtenstein & Mezière 2008 (BLUE protocol) [130]; Volpicelli et al. 2012 (lung ultrasound recommendations) [230]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A patient with a pulmonary artery catheter develops sudden massive haemoptysis after balloon inflation. What is the most likely complication?

options.B: Pulmonary embolism from the catheter tip
options.D: Pulmonary artery rupture
options.E: Pneumothorax

explanation: Pulmonary artery rupture is a rare but often fatal complication, especially with pulmonary hypertension, anticoagulation and distal catheter migration. Prevention includes careful balloon inflation, avoiding overwedging and keeping the catheter tip in a proximal position.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: When performing bronchoscopy through an endotracheal tube in a ventilated adult, which measure reduces complications?

options.A: Disconnecting the ventilator during the procedure
options.B: Increasing PEEP to 20 cmH2O to prevent derecruitment and hypoxaemia during suctioning
options.D: Using a 6.0-mm tube with a standard bronchoscope
options.E: An adequately sized tube (e.g. ≥8.0 mm), FiO2 1.0 and monitoring of pressures and volumes

explanation: A bronchoscope occupies a large portion of the tube lumen, increasing resistance, generating intrinsic PEEP and reducing tidal volume. Adequate tube size, 100% oxygen, a swivel adaptor, adjusted ventilator settings and limited suction time reduce hypoxaemia and barotrauma.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A hypotensive ventilated patient has a focused echocardiogram showing a dilated right ventricle (RV/LV ratio above 1), septal flattening and a small, hyperdynamic left ventricle. What does this suggest?

options.C: Left ventricular failure with high filling pressures and mitral regurgitation
options.D: Acute RV pressure overload, e.g. massive PE or ARDS-related cor pulmonale
options.E: Hypovolaemia

explanation: RV dilatation with septal flattening (D-shaped LV) indicates RV pressure overload. In ventilated patients, causes include PE, severe ARDS with high pressures and hypercapnia. Management includes reducing RV afterload, maintaining systemic pressure and treating the cause.
referenceText: Cecconi et al. 2014 (ESICM shock consensus) [34]; Konstantinides et al. 2020 (ESC pulmonary embolism) [117]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A relative telephones the ICU asking for detailed information about a competent patient who has asked that information not be shared. What is the correct response?

options.A: Disclose details if the caller sounds sincere
options.B: Respect the patient's wishes and do not disclose without consent
options.C: Share information with any caller claiming to be family
options.D: Post updates on social media
options.E: Give full details, because relatives have a right to know

explanation: Confidentiality is a core ethical and legal duty. Information may be shared with others only with the patient's consent, or in specific circumstances (lack of capacity with best-interest disclosure to involved relatives, legal requirements, or serious risk to others).
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What must be included for valid informed consent for a procedure such as percutaneous tracheostomy?

options.B: A signature on the standard form only, without any discussion of the risks or the alternatives
options.C: Information on nature, purpose, risks and alternatives, with voluntary consent from a capacitous patient
options.D: Consent from any staff member
options.E: Information only about benefits

explanation: Valid consent requires capacity, adequate information (including material risks and reasonable alternatives) and voluntariness. When patients lack capacity, decisions follow local law, involving surrogates and best interests; emergency treatment may proceed when delay would cause harm.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which ICU discharge practice is associated with increased in-hospital mortality and readmission?

options.A: Night-time or premature discharge from ICU due to bed pressure
options.B: Discharge with follow-up by an outreach team
options.D: Discharge during the day with a structured handover to the ward
options.E: Discharge after stabilisation of organ function

explanation: Night-time and premature discharges, often caused by bed shortages, are associated with higher mortality and readmission. Structured handovers, outreach or rapid response follow-up and step-down units mitigate risk.
referenceText: Valentin & Ferdinande 2011 (ESICM ICU requirements) [221]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which factor is associated with burnout syndrome among ICU staff?

options.B: Regular debriefing and peer support after difficult deaths
options.D: Shared decision-making
options.E: High workload, frequent end-of-life decisions, moral distress and conflict

explanation: Burnout is prevalent among ICU clinicians and is linked to workload, ethical conflicts, end-of-life care and poor team relationships. It affects patient safety and staff retention. Interventions include adequate staffing, debriefing, communication training and organisational support.
referenceText: Valentin & Ferdinande 2011 (ESICM ICU requirements) [221]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A study compares cardiac output measured by a new non-invasive monitor with thermodilution. Which analysis is most appropriate to assess agreement between the two methods?

options.B: Bland–Altman analysis of bias and limits of agreement
options.D: Chi-squared test
options.E: Pearson correlation coefficient alone, with a p-value

explanation: Correlation measures association, not agreement; two methods can be highly correlated yet disagree systematically. Bland–Altman plots show mean bias and 95% limits of agreement, and percentage error (commonly accepted below about 30% for cardiac output) assesses interchangeability.
referenceText: Altman 1991 (Practical Statistics for Medical Research) [2]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A patient with a radial arterial catheter develops a pale, cool hand with delayed capillary refill. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Insert a second catheter in the ulnar artery of the same hand to maintain monitoring
options.C: Remove the catheter promptly, assess perfusion and seek vascular input if needed
options.D: Leave the catheter and apply a warm compress
options.E: Flush the catheter with a large bolus of saline

explanation: Radial artery cannulation is generally safe, but thrombosis, vasospasm and embolism can cause hand ischaemia, particularly with high-dose vasopressors, small arteries or prolonged use. Signs of ischaemia require prompt catheter removal and assessment; rapid high-pressure flushes can cause retrograde cerebral embolism.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which four principles form the classic framework of medical ethics?

options.D: Beneficence, utility, consent and equity

explanation: Beauchamp and Childress' four principles guide ICU decisions. Strongest distractor: Paternalism conflicts with autonomy.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A competent patient refuses intubation knowing the consequences. What should the team do?

options.A: Seek an urgent court order before withholding intubation
options.B: Respect the refusal and provide comfort and other therapies
options.C: Intubate, as refusal of life-saving treatment implies impaired capacity
options.D: Sedate and intubate to save life

explanation: A competent adult may refuse life-sustaining treatment. Strongest distractor: Emergency doctrine does not override a competent refusal.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the doctrine of double effect?

options.A: A treatment may be given only if two senior doctors agree it is beneficial
options.B: Hastening death is acceptable if the patient explicitly requests it
options.C: Treatment must be doubled before withdrawal
options.D: An action with a good intended effect is allowed despite a foreseen bad effect

explanation: Opioids for symptoms are justified even if they may hasten death. Strongest distractor: Intention to hasten death is not permitted.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the best approach to terminal extubation regarding distress?

options.A: Pre-emptive opioids and sedatives titrated to comfort
options.B: Neuromuscular blockade before extubation to prevent visible gasping
options.D: No sedatives or opioids, to avoid any risk of hastening death

explanation: Comfort is priority; NMB masks distress and is inappropriate. Strongest distractor: NMB prevents assessment.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the principle of medical futility?

options.B: Treatment that cannot achieve its physiological or patient goals
options.D: Any treatment with less than a 50% chance of survival to discharge

explanation: Futility disputes should be addressed with communication and process. Strongest distractor: Cost does not define futility.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A family requests non-beneficial treatment. What is the best first step?

options.A: Withdraw treatment unilaterally, as doctors decide on futility
options.C: Family meeting to explore goals and values
options.D: Continue all treatment indefinitely, as the family has requested

explanation: Communication resolves most conflicts; mediation and ethics consult next. Strongest distractor: Unilateral withdrawal damages trust.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which communication approach improved family outcomes in the Lautrette 2007 study?

options.A: Shorter, more frequent meetings led by junior staff
options.B: Written information leaflets given instead of meetings
options.D: Proactive conference with VALUE approach and brochure

explanation: VALUE reduced PTSD, anxiety and depression in relatives. Strongest distractor: Written information alone was inferior.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What does SPIKES describe?

options.A: A protocol for breaking bad news
options.C: A structured bedside tool for assessing decision-making capacity
options.D: A triage tool

explanation: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy/summary. Strongest distractor: It is a communication protocol.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the dead donor rule?

options.A: Organ retrieval must not cause the donor's death
options.B: Donors must be certified dead for at least 24 hours before retrieval
options.D: Organs are taken before death declared

explanation: Ensures donation is ethical. Strongest distractor: DCD donors are allowed.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In DCD, why is the treating team separated from the transplant team?

options.A: To shorten warm ischaemia time and speed organ retrieval
options.B: To avoid conflict of interest in end-of-life decisions
options.C: To allow the transplant team to choose the time of withdrawal
options.D: Legal requirement for surgery

explanation: Withdrawal decision must be independent. Strongest distractor: Speed is not the reason.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the primary purpose of triage in mass casualty?

options.B: Treat the sickest patients first, regardless of their prognosis
options.D: Treat VIPs first

explanation: Utilitarian approach in disasters. Strongest distractor: Sickest first ignores benefit.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A patient requests treatment details be hidden from family. What should the doctor do?

options.D: Ignore request

explanation: Confidentiality is core unless there is a risk to others. Strongest distractor: Family disclosure breaches confidentiality.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: When may confidentiality be broken?

options.A: To prevent serious harm to others or when law requires
options.B: Never; confidentiality is absolute in all circumstances
options.D: When the next of kin requests the information

explanation: Exceptions: public health notification, court order, serious harm. Strongest distractor: Family request does not justify disclosure.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A medication error causes harm. What should the doctor do?

options.C: Disclose only if the patient or family asks directly
options.D: Disclose honestly and apologise

explanation: Duty of candour. Strongest distractor: Concealment is unethical.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is a root cause analysis?

options.B: An audit of individual staff performance and competence
options.D: Disciplinary process

explanation: RCA identifies system failures. Strongest distractor: It is not disciplinary.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the Swiss cheese model?

options.B: Errors occur when multiple defence layers fail
options.D: Most errors are caused by a single careless individual

explanation: Reason's model for system safety. Strongest distractor: Single-person focus misses systems.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the intensivist-to-patient effect on outcomes?

options.B: No effect, as long as a physician is available by phone
options.D: Only nurses matter

explanation: Pronovost 2002 meta-analysis. Strongest distractor: Staffing matters.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which nurse-to-patient ratio is typical for ventilated patients?
explanation: Intensive care societies recommend 1:1 for level 3. Strongest distractor: 1:4 is ward level.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is burnout among ICU staff?

options.A: Physical fatigue that resolves after rest from night shifts
options.C: Emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced accomplishment
options.D: Depression only

explanation: Maslach triad. Strongest distractor: It is more than fatigue.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is moral distress?

options.B: Knowing the right action but constrained from taking it
options.D: Persistent disagreement with a colleague about a diagnosis

explanation: Common among ICU nurses. Strongest distractor: It is not grief.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the ethical principle of justice in ICU?

options.B: Respecting each patient's own choice of treatment
options.D: Avoiding harm

explanation: Applies to triage and admission. Strongest distractor: Respect for choice is autonomy.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the principle of proportionality in ICU?

options.B: Use maximal therapy whenever survival is possible
options.D: Treat all equally

explanation: Guides limitation of treatment. Strongest distractor: Maximum therapy may be disproportionate.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: When is consent not required?

options.B: For all routine ICU procedures once the patient is admitted
options.D: Emergency treatment to save life when patient lacks capacity

explanation: Implied consent in emergencies. Strongest distractor: Elective procedures need consent.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: A patient's religion conflicts with blood transfusion. What is the approach?

options.B: Seek a court order immediately so transfusion can proceed
options.C: Respect refusal; use blood conservation strategies
options.D: Transfuse anyway

explanation: Competent refusal respected. Strongest distractor: Transfusing against refusal is assault.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is a time-limited trial?

options.C: Agreement to use therapy for a defined period and reassess
options.D: Open-ended full treatment until the patient recovers

explanation: Helps with prognostic uncertainty. Strongest distractor: It has a defined endpoint.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which statement on DNR orders is correct?

options.D: DNR does not mean do not treat

explanation: Other treatments remain appropriate. Strongest distractor: DNR is CPR-specific.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the role of an ethics committee?

options.D: Making binding decisions that the treating team must follow

explanation: Advisory not binding. Strongest distractor: Decisions are not binding.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which factor predicts family dissatisfaction?

options.A: A long ICU stay with many invasive procedures
options.D: Use of ventilator

explanation: Consistency is key. Strongest distractor: Long stay alone is not the main factor.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the primary goal of palliative care in ICU?

options.A: Relieve suffering and improve quality of life
options.C: Prolong life with all available therapies
options.D: Reduce costs

explanation: Can be integrated with curative care. Strongest distractor: Hastening death is not the goal.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the definition of euthanasia?

options.A: Withdrawing a treatment that is no longer beneficial
options.C: Intentional act to end life to relieve suffering
options.D: Giving opioids for pain

explanation: Distinct from withdrawal. Strongest distractor: Withdrawal is not euthanasia.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What does Egyptian law state about euthanasia?

options.A: It is permitted for terminal illness
options.D: It is permitted with court approval

explanation: Egyptian law and Islamic jurisprudence prohibit euthanasia. Strongest distractor: No consent-based exception exists.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: In Islamic ethics, what is the position on withdrawing futile life support?

options.C: Permissible only if every family member agrees to it
options.D: Permissible when treatment is futile per medical judgement

explanation: Fatwas permit withdrawal of futile treatment. Strongest distractor: It is not always forbidden.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the definition of a sentinel event?

options.A: Unexpected occurrence causing death or serious harm
options.C: An expected, recognised complication of a procedure
options.D: Near miss

explanation: Requires investigation. Strongest distractor: Near misses do not cause harm.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is a near miss?

options.A: A recognised complication that caused temporary harm
options.C: Error that did not reach the patient or cause harm
options.D: Death

explanation: Valuable for learning. Strongest distractor: It does not cause harm.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which strategy improves handover?

options.D: Structured tools like I-PASS

explanation: I-PASS reduced medical errors. Strongest distractor: Unstructured handover increases errors.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which early warning score is commonly used?

options.D: SAPS

explanation: NEWS2 identifies deteriorating patients. Strongest distractor: APACHE is a severity score.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which score is used for ICU severity and mortality prediction?

options.D: Glasgow Coma Scale

explanation: Calculated in first 24 h. Strongest distractor: NEWS2 is for wards.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is the standardised mortality ratio?

options.A: Predicted deaths divided by observed deaths
options.B: Observed deaths divided by predicted deaths
options.D: Deaths per 100 admissions

explanation: SMR <1 indicates better than expected. Strongest distractor: Inverted ratio is incorrect.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: What is normothermic regional perfusion?

options.B: Machine perfusion of the isolated heart after retrieval
options.D: ECMO-based perfusion of organs after DCD

explanation: Improves graft outcomes. Strongest distractor: It is not cooling.

setTitle: Ethics, End-of-Life Care, ICU Organisation, Research
stem: Which complication is characteristic of DCD liver grafts compared with DBD grafts?

options.A: Hyperacute antibody-mediated rejection in the first hours
options.D: Higher rate of CMV disease in the recipient

explanation: Warm ischaemia during DCD injures the biliary epithelium; NRP and machine perfusion reduce this risk. Strongest distractor: Hyperacute rejection relates to preformed antibodies, not donor type.
